intro: You don't need a budget to get good at gemini api free tier models. You need a map of the free tools, and an honest read on the trade-offs between them. Here's that map — researched, written and fact-checked by the same engine that publishes this blog.

We'll walk through Gemini API Free Tier, Openrouter Free Models, Choosing a Free LLM for a Blog, and Automate the boring parts — and finish with the questions people actually ask, so you can check before you buy anything. You shouldn't have to buy anything.

sections.heading: Gemini API Free Tier
paragraphs: Here's the part most people get wrong. Google's Gemini API has a free tier with per-minute and per-day model quotas — no credit card required.

Which, in day-to-day terms, means: You sign in with a Google account, create a key in AI Studio, and call the models over an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The free tier's rate limits are more than enough for a blog that writes a few posts a day, and the paid tier is only for when you outgrow the quotas.
The links in the sources section go straight to the primary docs.
bullets: Create a Google AI Studio API key
Point any OpenAI-compatible client at the Gemini OpenAI endpoint
Set LLM_BASE_URL, LLM_API_KEY and LLM_MODEL and this engine writes with it

sections.heading: Openrouter Free Models
paragraphs: First, the thing that actually matters: OpenRouter aggregates dozens of model providers behind one API, and a set of models carry a ':free' suffix with no credit card required.

Concretely: One key, one endpoint, many backends — you can switch models in a config line and keep the same code. The free models rotate, but the pattern is stable: check the model list, pick the ones marked free, done.
For a personal project or side business, this covers you without breaking a sweat.

sections.heading: Choosing a Free LLM for a Blog
paragraphs: Here's the part most people get wrong. For an autonomous blog the right model is the one that hits the free quotas comfortably while sounding like a person.

The upshot: A few posts a day uses a tiny fraction of any free tier's daily allowance. The practical recipe: pick one primary provider for reliability, keep a second as fallback in an env var, and let the engine fall back to its template writer if both fail — the blog never misses a publish date.
For a personal project or side business, this covers you without breaking a sweat.

sections.heading: Automate the boring parts
paragraphs: Here's the part most people get wrong. Anything you do twice by hand should become a script. That's the entire discipline of free automation.

In other words: A cron expression, a webhook, or a scheduled workflow costs nothing to run and buys back an hour every week. Start with one small automation — a nightly backup, a feed check, a deploy on push — and add more only when the first one proves itself.
If you only do one thing today, make it this one.
